E1720.summary: In a passage from Julian, the art whose pre-eminent power is to impart health, understood as symmetry or equilibrium of nature.
E1720.body: Quoted from Julian: “health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature, which it is the pre-eminent power of the Telestic art to impart, ordering all things by the unity within” [IV.3 ¶30]. So the art imparts equilibrium by ordering everything through an inner unity.

E1721.summary: The first grade of initiation: being initiated, while ascending, by the perfective gods.
E1721.body: In Socrates in the Phaedrus (n15 cites Proclus): “we are initiated (teleioumetha) in ascending by the perfective gods” [II.4 ¶23]. The record treats this as the first grade of the ascent.

E1722.summary: Cited by Atwood as places where bodily healing was widely practised with minor physico-magical arts.
E1722.body: Atwood cites the temples of Esculapius to show that bodily healing was widely practised there with the minor physico-magical arts [II.2 ¶5].

E1723.summary: Atwood's name for the present age's idol of worldly usefulness, set up by opinion, which even its worshippers feel to be insufficient.
E1723.body: Atwood speaks of “that earth-born goddess of temporal Utility, which opinion has set up” [IV.3 ¶50]: the present age's idol of worldly usefulness and advantage. She says even its votaries feel it falls short.

E1724.summary: A threefold principle: the thing an offering in the vessel is dedicated to, and the term in the Theosophist's formula for reduction to the Monad.
E1724.body:
An ancient Adeptus (Grasseus, n26) speaks of “a holy oblation or present, dedicated to the Ternary” [III.2 ¶25]. The passage does not explain the term.

The Theosophist gives a formula: “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary” [IV.2 ¶18], that is, reduce it to the Monad by rejecting the Binary. In the same paragraph, at the incarnation the four elements “were united to their eternal Unity and Ternarius” [IV.2 ¶18].

E1725.summary: The red root, which the wise sometimes call Magnesia, and Salt once it has been purified.
E1725.body: Atwood names Terra Adamica as the red root. She says it is “called sometimes Magnesia by the wise, and Salt after the purification” [I.3 n52]. So it = Magnesia, and = Salt after purification.

E1726.summary: The gross, earthy part of metals. It binds their central light and must be purged; the Stone removes it from them.
E1726.body: Atwood says metals cannot work “unless they be first purged from their terrestreity” [I.2 ¶49]. Their earthiness overpowers their spirit. In a footnote she says the central light “in metalline bodies is more especially bound on account of their terrestreity” [I.3 n49]. Khunrath, quoted, says the Stone acts on metals by “depriving its terrestreity and foreign oxides” [IV.3 ¶28].

E1727.summary: In the Appendix, the sensuous life: it represents the Animal Kingdom and dominates the head in man.
E1727.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “The Terrestrial is the sensuous and represents the Animal Kingdom. In man it is dominating the head.” [APP ¶32]. The reader's record adds that it typifies the highest life man must not aspire to. This point is not in the quoted words.

E1728.summary: In Eudoxus, turning the Spirit into earth: the only operation of the Fourth Key, done by boiling.
E1728.body: Eudoxus, quoted: “The terrification of the Spirit is the only operation of this work” [IV.3 ¶12]. This is the Fourth Key, and the operation is done by boiling. The same paragraph describes it as the need “to corporify the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12], and as coagulation by the Sulphur. Making the Spirit earthy, giving it a body and coagulating it are apparently one operation.

E1730.summary: The fourfold drawn by the Art from three heads. It is identified with the Conjunction and called the source of ever-flowing Nature; such a being was the basis of the philosophic stone.
E1730.body:
Atwood calls the Tetractys a fourfold, “drawn from three heads by the obstetric hand of the physico-chemical Art” [III.3 ¶35]. She also calls it “Perennial nature’s fountain, cause, and root” [III.3 ¶34]. She identifies it with the consummating Conjunction: “the Conjunction, by Ripley called tetraptive, that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33]. The records also call it indissoluble and the source of wisdom.

She also says “the physical Tetractys springs through the contrite experience into life” [III.3 ¶72]. It springs out of the Calx, with prolific attributes and lasting fruits.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says Pythagorus's mystic Tetractys was obtained by the theurgic process of APP ¶107. It is “the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature” [APP ¶108], and such an ens was the basis of the philosophic stone.

E1731.summary: Early Greek philosopher who sought eastern wisdom. Atwood reads his Water as the Matter itself, not common water.
E1731.body: Atwood names Thales, with Pythagoras, among early Greeks who sought eastern wisdom and whose writings are lost [I.1 ¶12]. She says his water, from which all is generated, is not common water [I.2 ¶43]. He “teaches that all beings have their beginning from water” [III.2 ¶33]. He names the principle after its first material appearance, so he differs from the others only in expression [III.2 ¶34–35]. She identifies “the Water of Thales” with the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. She reads his deed about inscribing the circle as symbolic, not a plain demonstration [III.2 ¶44].

E1732.summary: A work Atwood cites to show that blood is the principal matter of each thing.
E1732.body: Atwood cites it for the line “For blood is the principle matter of each thing” [II.1 ¶15, II.1 n14].

E1733.summary: A collection Atwood calls “an esteemed work.” She cites it for an annotated Sommaire, for Picus' de Auro, and for the Prosopoiae of the Stone.
E1733.body: Atwood calls the Theatrum Chemicum an esteemed work. It contains a translation of the Sommaire with important annotations, and she also cites it for Picus' de Auro [I.1 ¶58, I.1 n69]. From vol. 3, p. 763 she takes the Prosopoiae of the Stone, which she calls instructive and elegant. It begins “Terra mihi corpus, vires mihi praestitit ignis” [III.3 ¶8, III.3 n2], which means: Earth gave me my body, fire gave me my powers (our translation).

E1734.summary: Cited for the initiate's perplexity until the conductor opens the vestibule.
E1734.body: Quoted in a footnote: “the initiated is seized at first with solicitude and perplexity” [II.3 n37]. This lasts until the conductor opens the vestibule. Atwood uses the passage to support her account of initiation.

E1735.summary: In the Appendix, the only true government. Atwood accepts this as a great truth but says it needs a matching surface.
E1735.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood takes up the claim that theocracy is the only true government (Kirchberger for de St Martin). She endorses it as a great truth, but says it needs a matching surface: “the world’s surface can only be governed by the center from which it is derived --- that is, its king” [APP ¶112].

E1736.summary: Science that is everywhere condemned. Atwood says none exists today, because the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared.
E1736.body: Atwood: “Theoretic science is everywhere condemned; but there is no such thing at this day” [IV.4 ¶28]. Her reason is that the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared.

E1737.summary: Atwood's word for divine, ultimate knowledge grounded in experiment. She says it opens a wider plane than the theological and contrasts it with the merely intellectual.
E1737.body: Atwood calls the subjects of the Poemander and Asclepias “theosophic and ultimate” [I.1 ¶7]: they concern divine capabilities, not physical ground. She hopes to show that “the most famous schools of theosophy have in all ages been based on a similar experimental ground” [I.1 ¶17]. Of Boehme she says the ancient wisdom was “Revealed anew, it will be observed, theosophically, but not intellectually.” [I.1 ¶70]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Theosophic light opens him at a much wider plane of thought than the Theological.” [APP ¶118]. There she uses the word for the light of the higher Mystics, and also for the doctrine of the Neo-Platonists and Behmen.

E1738.summary: A theosophical authority Atwood quotes and endorses. A footnote at one place names him as Khunrath.
E1738.body: Atwood quotes the theosophist on the hostile reception that the wrathful outer life gives the new light, and on love's victory over it: “The wrathfulness is mightily exasperated by this appearance of love, says the theosophist” [I.3 n69]. She also uses him, with approval, on Adam and the fall, the two fires, the tincturing of Mercury, the Two Natures, the Mercury as worker and the Artist's role. On this she quotes “Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.” [IV.3 ¶38]. In Amp. Sap. Etern. the Theosophist (footnote: Khunrath) gives the formula “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary, through the rejection of the Binary, to the simplicity of the Monad” [IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 n14]. Atwood then explains it.

E1739.summary: In Norton, the “hidden treasure” of the old clerks, identified with the Fourth House or its Lord.
E1739.body: Norton, quoted: “For the Lord of the Fourth House likewise be it done; For that is Thesaurum absconditum of old clerkes” [IV.2 ¶34]. The Latin means “hidden treasure” (our translation). The verse is ambiguous: the treasure may be the Fourth House itself or its Lord.

E1740.summary: Unnamed philosophers who supply the mountain allegory. Atwood qualifies them: their promises of gold drew futile public searches.
E1740.body: Atwood gives their allegory of the mountain: wind, earthquake, fire, calm, then the tincture. It begins “When you have discovered the mountain, the first miracle that will appear is this” [II.3 ¶33]. She qualifies their use: their promises of gold drew the public into futile searches [II.3 ¶34].

E1741.summary: Greek philosophers whose contradictory statements about Matter Atwood explains and defends, comparing them with the Hermetic adepts.
E1741.body: These Greeks say contradictory things about Matter: that it is one and all, everywhere and nowhere. Atwood explains and defends these statements and compares them with the Hermetic adepts [III.2 ¶51, III.2 ¶52].

E1742.summary: The art of purifying and informing the Mind. Through purification it turns the whole being into inner light and makes the divine Matter manifest in arcane visions.
E1742.body:
Atwood says “the Theurgic Art professed a power of purifying and informing the Mind much more beneficial and lasting” than bodily medicine [III.1 ¶11]. By purifying and subduing the passions it turns the whole hypostasis into inner light. Its practitioners consulted the divine intellect only about purification, liberation and the salvation of life [III.1 ¶11].

In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses, the pure divine Matter is shown “by means of the Theurgic Art it is made manifest and imparted through arcane and blessed visions” [III.2 ¶49].

The Alexandrian philosophers practised it, “each professing a genuine knowledge of the Theurgic art, and experimental physics on the Hermetic ground” [I.1 ¶27]. Later, “Theurgic rites, no longer holy, were proscribed” [I.1 ¶30].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says numbers are personally represented in this art, “by which spirit is added to spirit and multiplied as offspring” [APP ¶107].

E1743.summary: Ancient rites aimed at the experience of truth, ordered by intellectual canons. Atwood draws on their kinds of invocation to defend prayer.
E1743.body: Iamblicus, quoted: “Theurgic rites conspiring to this end were scientifically disposed and early defined by intellectual canons” [II.2 ¶13]. The end is the experience of truth. Atwood draws on “the different kinds of invocation which were employed by the ancients in their celebration of Theurgic rites” [III.4 ¶23] in defending prayer.

E1744.summary: Sacrifice whose end is conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect. It goes together with adoration and prayer.
E1744.body: Atwood: “the end of Theurgic sacrifice is a conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect” [III.4 ¶25]. She connects it with adoration and prayer.

E1745.summary: In Iamblichus, the soul's union with the Divine nature. Ineffable works and symbols bring it about, not intellectual perception.
E1745.body: Iamblichus, quoted: the soul's union with the Divine nature comes about through “the perfect efficacy of ineffable works” and symbols, not through intellectual perception [II.4 ¶31].

E1746.summary: In Iamblichus, those to whom the gods show a Fire visible to itself.
E1746.body: Iamblichus, quoted: “they exhibit to Theurgists a Fire which is itself, to itself, visible” [II.4 ¶29].

E1747.summary: Practitioners of theurgy. Proclus is cited saying they place their chief hopes of salvation in the Elysian fountains.
E1747.body: Atwood reports Proclus as saying the Theurgists place their chief hopes of salvation in the Elysian fountains [II.4 ¶16].

E1748.summary: The Greek name for the Hermetic Art. Through it the soul concentrates its vitality, purifies its essence and rises by degrees to knowledge of the First Cause.
E1748.body:
Atwood: “Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy” [II.2 ¶3]. So Theurgy = the Hermetic Art. She calls it the practice of the Mysteries. Through it, “through their Theurgic disciplines” [II.2 ¶6], Theurgists shared in the Wisdom of true Being. “The Neoplatonists wrote largely of the Theurgical art” [II.2 ¶9].

Its aim was to concentrate vitality, turn the spiritual eye, purify and analyse the whole essence, and draw out and know the true Efficient: “this was their object and the Art of Theurgy” [II.3 ¶5]. She says this ascent needs those means: “by Theurgic rites, an ascent was made through appropriate media and a gradual assimilation, which without these could not be effected, to the knowledge of the First Cause” [II.4 ¶56]. So whoever seeks the First Principle “must be theurgically prepared” [III.3 ¶59]. That passage does not define the preparation further.

E1749.summary: In Jacob Boehme, what proceeds by virtue of the warmth (fire) in the blood.
E1749.body: Jacob Boehme, quoted: “in the virtue of the warmth, the Thin Water of Life proceedeth” [III.3 ¶24]. The warmth is the fire in the blood.

E1750.summary: Something mesmerists reach without knowing how to alter and amend it. It is not further defined.
E1750.body: Atwood says mesmerists reach it, but “without the important knowledge how to alter and amend the Thing” [III.1 ¶8]. The capital letters suggest a technical sense, but the passage does not define it.
